1.notes: Hint 2 reads: "Nigeria has belonged to the continental bodies and to the oil exporters' club for decades, so it could not be newly admitted to them in 2014. OPEC also has no permanent or non-permanent seats." "The continental bodies" covers both B (AU) and C (OAU), and the second sentence covers D (OPEC), so hint 2 eliminates all three distractors in one go, leaving only A. Hint 3 then says: "Of the world body and the continental body, which one has a council where five countries hold their seats permanently and the rest are elected for two years?" This presents two live options, but by hint 2's own reasoning nothing except the UN is still live, so the answer was already handed over a hint early and hint 3 does no real narrowing.
1.fix: Hint 2: "The Organization of African Unity had already been replaced by the African Union in 2002, so it did not exist in 2014. OPEC also has no permanent or non-permanent seats." This leaves exactly the UN and the AU live, which matches hint 3's "world body and the continental body" as written, so hint 3 can stay unchanged.

3.notes: Hint 2 reads: "The Supreme Military Council was the name used by the regimes from 1966 up to 1985, and the Provisional Ruling Council was the name used from 1993." Gowon (1966-1975) and Buhari (1983-1985) both sit under the SMC window, and Abacha sits under the PRC window, so this one sentence eliminates all three distractors (A, C, D), leaving only Babangida. Hint 3, "Of the leaders left, who came to power that year?", has nothing left to narrow at that point, so the answer is effectively given away in hint 2 rather than built up to across three hints.
3.fix: Hint 2: "The Provisional Ruling Council was the name used from 1993, under Abacha, which is too late. Gowon's regime, from 1966 to 1975, also used the Supreme Military Council, long before the AFRC existed." Hint 3: "Two remain, Babangida and Buhari, who followed one after the other in the 1980s. The AFRC was set up in August 1985, after a coup that ended one of their regimes. Which one lost power that month, and which one set up the AFRC in its place?"

4.notes: Hint 2 reads: "Chad and Libya had no atomic bombs to test. Nigeria's break with Israel came in 1973, over a war in the Middle East." This names and eliminates B, C and D together, leaving only France live. Hint 3 then opens "Two remain.", which is a false statement given hint 2's own reasoning: no distractor is still live at that point, only the correct answer is, so "two remain" contradicts the elimination just performed one hint earlier. Quote: "Two remain. Which of them ruled Algeria in 1960, when the bombs were tested in the Algerian part of the Sahara?"
4.fix: Hint 2: "Chad and Libya had no atomic bombs to test in the early 1960s." Hint 3: "Two remain, France and Israel. Nigeria's break with one of them came in 1973, over a war in the Middle East. Which one ruled Algeria in 1960, when the bomb was tested there?"

24.notes: Hint 3 fails the 'without thinking' test. After hint 2 eliminates House of Lords and House of Commons, the only two options left are C. Congress and D. National Assembly. Hint 3 reads: 'Two remain. Recall what the US Senate and the US House of Representatives are called together.' The answer to that literal question is the word 'Congress', which is exactly the text of option C. There is no distinguishing step or elimination left to do: a student who recalls the vocabulary term has the full answer with zero comparison between the two remaining options, unlike the standard's own example (hint 3 pointing to a body shape, which the student must still map onto an insect name).
24.fix: Two remain, one used for Nigeria and one used for the USA. Which of the two names is the one Nigeria gives to its own federal legislature, so that the other one is left for the USA?

34.notes: Hint 3 says: 'Of the two left, does the doctrine aim to build up one arm, or to stop power being misused?' This is a direct paraphrase of the two remaining options, not a prompt to reason: 'build up one arm' restates option A ('Strengthening the executive') and 'stop power being misused' restates option B ('Preventing abuse of power') almost word for word. Combined with hint 2, which already frames the doctrine as the answer to the danger of concentrated power, a student can match the paraphrase to option B without weighing any evidence. This fails the hint 3 test: read alone, it lets the student answer without thinking.
34.fix: Weakening one arm or placing one arm above the others would undo the balance the idea is built on, so set those aside. Of the two left, think about what checks such as the veto, legislative oversight and judicial review are actually used for: growing one arm's reach, or stopping any arm from acting without another arm able to stop it.
